nature-gov-184.title: Indigenous peoples: who they are, and who decides
nature-gov-184.text: There are some 5,000 distinct Indigenous peoples, living on every inhabited continent and in every climate zone people live in. Yet no one agrees on exactly who counts. The UN has adopted no definition. Its Permanent Forum holds that any single definition would include too many or too few. Most accounts point to four marks. People identify themselves as Indigenous and differ culturally from others in their state. They have a special bond with their traditional territory and share a history of domination. Most are minorities where they live. Many states avoid the term altogether, using labels such as "scheduled tribes" in India or "national minorities" in China. Whether particular groups in Africa or Asia count as Indigenous is disputed. History explains much of their position. Europeans justified colonizing Indigenous lands partly by calling them terra nullius, "no one's land." Since 2002, Indigenous environmental rights have gained international recognition. Few countries respect them in practice.

nature-gov-168.title: Environmental justice: who lives next to the dump?
nature-gov-168.text: In 1982, residents of Warren County, North Carolina, protested a landfill for toxic PCB chemicals. Six weeks of protest led to over 500 arrests. That fight helped launch the environmental justice movement in the United States. Shaped by the civil rights movement, it opposes harm done to poor or marginalized communities by waste, mining and other land uses that bring them no benefit. Its early focus was race, covered in {{ref:nature-gov-173}}. A United Church of Christ study found that race was the most important factor predicting where US hazardous waste facilities were placed. Hundreds of studies from the movement argue that exposure to environmental harm is unequally distributed. The US Environmental Protection Agency now defines environmental justice as fair treatment and meaningful involvement of all people in environmental laws and policies. That covers every race, color, national origin and income. The movement went global in the 1980s and 1990s. Tighter waste rules in rich countries sent a surge of hazardous waste to the Global South. It has since spawned new ideas, among them the debt rich nations may owe poor ones and the unequal burden of climate change. It overlaps with campaigns for Indigenous rights to land and for a human right to a clean environment.

nature-gov-227.title: Political ecology: power and the environment
nature-gov-227.text: Farmers eroding their soil looks like a local failure. Piers Blaikie dug deeper. His work on the social and political roots of soil erosion showed that problems blamed on local misuse often stem from the wider political and economic context. That insight is the heart of political ecology, the study of how political, economic and social forces shape environmental problems and climate change. Unlike conventional ecology, it puts power relations at the center. A core assumption is that environmental change does not hit society evenly. Political, social and economic differences shape who pays the costs and who reaps the benefits. The field joins ecological social science with political economy. It covers degradation and marginalization, fights over resources, conservation and control, and social movements. It traces today's uneven burdens back to policies and power rooted in colonialism. Frank Thone coined the English term in 1935, and the anthropologist Eric R. Wolf revived it in 1972. Not everyone is convinced. Critics such as Vayda and Walters argue it assumes politics matters before showing it, and propose "event ecology" instead.

nature-gov-176.title: Traditional ecological knowledge
nature-gov-176.text: Long before weather forecasts, people read the wind, the blooming of plants and the arrival of birds. Traditional ecological knowledge, or TEK, is that kind of understanding. It is knowledge, practice and belief about how living things, people included, relate to each other and their surroundings. It builds up over generations and passes on through culture. It guides everyday needs such as weather reading, medicine, water management, farming, hunting, fishing and naming living things. It is not one universal system. It is a family of practices tied to particular places and worldviews. It rests on long observation and experience rather than standardized experiments, and that has fueled debate over its use in management. Combined with science, though, it can supply long-term records that would otherwise be missing. A 1987 UN report, described in {{ref:nature-hist-004}}, said Indigenous and tribal ways of life could teach modern societies how to manage forest, mountain and dryland ecosystems. TEK is usually oral, so it may lack the written records that legal claims require. Whether Indigenous peoples hold intellectual property rights over it is still debated in international law. Some critics call the term itself an appropriation. Climate change adds a threat, making the signs in nature that TEK relies on less dependable.

nature-gov-209.title: Extractivism: digging up and shipping out
nature-gov-209.text: Gold, oil, lumber, water and food leave a region raw and get processed somewhere else. Extractivism is the removal of large amounts of natural resources, mainly for export, with little or no processing. The term was coined in Portuguese, "extractivismo," in 1996 to describe profit-driven exploitation of Brazil's forests. The practice is far older. For over 500 years, colonies in Africa, Asia and the Americas shipped resources to imperial centers. Today transnational corporations are the main actors, helped by weak governance in economies that depend on resources. It is common across the Global South and the Arctic, and in neglected, heavily polluted pockets of the Global North. Taken fast enough, even renewable resources become non-renewable, because nature cannot replace them in time. Local and especially Indigenous communities often resist, because it uproots them or degrades their lives.

nature-gov-217.title: Land law: who may use, sell or fence the ground
nature-gov-217.text: Rights to land are so basic that they arise even without a government. In the American West, miners' claim clubs enforced their own rules. Land law is the branch of law covering the rights to use land, transfer it, or keep others off it. Land is often called real estate or real property, as distinct from personal belongings. One person's burden on land, such as a neighbor's right of way, may be another person's right. Squatting, living on land without owning it, happens all over the world. Land reform means government policies that take or redistribute land. Where customary law rules, customary land is the main form of ownership. In common-law countries, Indigenous peoples' claims to land have their own legal name, described in {{ref:nature-gov-216}}.

nature-gov-199.title: Ecological debt: what the North owes the South
nature-gov-199.text: At the 1992 summit in Rio, campaign groups drafted a Debt Treaty demanding compensation for 500 years of damage. No international institution ever recognized it. Their claim was ecological debt: the idea that the Global North owes the Global South for past environmental injustice, such as resource plunder, habitat damage and pollution. It has two parts. One is damage a country does to others or to shared ecosystems. The other is its use of ecosystems at the expense of other countries' fair share. The German ecofeminist Eva Quistorp first used the term in a 1985 booklet. Early reports split on approach: a Chilean one treated it in moral terms, a Swedish one tried to price it. At the 2009 Copenhagen talks, vulnerable countries demanded reparations for decades of excess pollution, and the US envoy flatly rejected the idea. Climate debt, the best-developed attempt to measure it, splits into adaptation debt and emissions debt. Proposals to settle it include canceling poor countries' financial debts. Almost everything about it is disputed, and some warn it risks putting a price on nature.

nature-es-105.title: Biopiracy: patenting other people's knowledge
nature-es-105.text: Nearly one third of the small-molecule drugs the US FDA approved between 1981 and 2014 were natural products or derived from them. Nature's chemistry is valuable, and so is the local knowledge that points to it. Biopiracy is taking the genetic resources and knowledge of farming and Indigenous communities without permission, to win monopoly control through patents. Pat Mooney, founder of ETC Group, coined the term in the early 1990s. A company patent can bar anyone, even the Indigenous group itself, from using or selling the resource. Critics say the TRIPS trade agreement treats knowledge as private property and recognizes inventions only if they can make industrial profit. The 1992 Biodiversity Convention required host-country consent and fair sharing of benefits, and the 2010 Nagoya Protocol made this concrete. The unintended result was blocked research. Critics call both biopiracy and the search for useful compounds modern extractivism.

nature-gov-185.title: Indigenous land stewardship
nature-gov-185.text: At least 37% of the world's remaining natural lands lie within Indigenous territories. Where Indigenous peoples hold secure title, their care of the land benefits everyone. A report by the research group WRI says such lands generate billions, sometimes trillions, of dollars in benefits, such as carbon storage, cleaner air and clean water. Deforestation on them is low. They cut greenhouse gas emissions, and their rooted soils limit erosion and flooding. One popular claim does not hold up. The often-repeated figure that Indigenous peoples steward 80% of the world's biodiversity was found baseless by a 2024 study in Nature.

nature-gov-186.title: Climate change and Indigenous peoples
nature-gov-186.text: The Arctic is warming at twice the global rate, and its Indigenous nations face challenges with no precedent. Pacific islands have already been lost to rising seas, displacing and killing Indigenous people. Climate change falls harder on Indigenous peoples than on others. There are over 370 million Indigenous people in more than 90 countries, and about 22% of the planet's land is Indigenous territory. Indigenous farmers have long timed crops by wind direction, flowering and bird migration, signs that a changing climate scrambles. Some Indigenous scholars see climate change as an intensification of settler colonialism's effects. Their knowledge is also an asset. It detects local impacts where scientific models often fail, and programs shaped with Indigenous input draw more participation. Yet Indigenous people in the Ecuadorian Amazon were left out of a 2005 forest-carbon project despite suffering deforestation's effects.

nature-gov-198.title: Ecocide: killing the home
nature-gov-198.text: The word joins Greek oikos, "home," and Latin caedere, "to kill." Ecocide is the destruction of the environment by humans. Olof Palme popularized the term at the 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment. He accused the United States of ecocide in Vietnam. There the US Air Force sprayed 20 million gallons of herbicides such as Agent Orange on 6 million acres of forest and crops. In 2021 an expert panel defined it as unlawful or wanton acts committed knowing they are substantially likely to cause severe and widespread or long-term damage. Common causes include war, pollution, reckless overexploitation and industrial disasters. The International Criminal Court covers environmental damage only in wartime. Ten countries have made peacetime ecocide a crime, and campaigners want the court to try it. Supporters see a deterrent to corporations driving climate change. Others doubt it would touch the crisis's root causes. Destroying a landscape can also be cultural genocide, ending a people's way of life.

nature-gov-202.title: Environmental conflict: fighting over nature's spoils
nature-gov-202.text: As of April 2020, the Environmental Justice Atlas had documented 3,100 environmental conflicts worldwide, and many more go unrecorded. An environmental conflict is a social clash caused by environmental damage or by unequal sharing of environmental resources. Such conflicts are rooted in the industrial economy. With less than 10% of materials and energy recycled, extraction keeps pushing into new frontiers. A study of over 2743 conflicts found mining the most contested sector, at 21%. Fossil energy followed at 17%, biomass and land use at 15%, and water at 14%. Defenders were killed in 13% of cases. Poor countries see more fights over conservation, water and land. In rich countries almost half concern waste, tourism, nuclear power and infrastructure. Around 17% end in a justice "success," such as stopping a project. The best predictor of resolving one is proper consultation with every party.

nature-gov-220.title: Procedural justice: fair process, not just fair results
nature-gov-220.text: People often accept a decision they dislike if they feel they were heard. Research by Tom R. Tyler found that simply giving people a voice, even one that changes nothing, can make a process feel fair. Procedural justice is fairness in how disputes are settled and resources shared. It differs from distributive justice, which asks whether outcomes are fair, and retributive justice, which asks whether punishment is fair. In 1976 Gerald Leventhal proposed six tests for a fair procedure: consistency, lack of bias, accuracy, the chance to correct errors, representativeness and ethics. Hearing all parties before deciding is a basic step. In energy and environmental matters, it means access to information and real participation. In law it appears as due process in the US and natural justice elsewhere.

nature-gov-162.title: Climate justice: those who suffer most did least
nature-gov-162.text: Pakistan produces less than 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Its 2022 floods affected over 33 million people. That mismatch is the core of climate justice, a branch of environmental justice concerned with how unequally climate change harms marginalized and vulnerable people. It seeks to share fairly both the burdens of climate change and the work of cutting emissions. The responsibility is lopsided. Those who gained most from industrialization, such as coal, oil and gas businesses, are seen as most responsible for the carbon dioxide in the air. The richest 1% of people cause twice the emissions of the poorest 50%. Many of the people hit hardest did least to cause the problem. When they are also hurt by the responses to climate change, the result is called the "triple injustice." Views of climate justice fall into two camps. One focuses on fair, inclusive decision-making. The other asks who bears the costs. Lawsuits are one tool: a 2017 UN Environment Programme report counted 894 climate legal actions worldwide. The term is used in many ways, and its meanings are disputed. So is the question of whether capitalism itself is a root cause.

nature-gov-193.title: Climate change and poverty
nature-gov-193.text: For a poor household, one disaster, bad harvest or illness can be crippling. That fragility is why climate change hits poor people and developing countries hardest. The UN Development Programme says developing countries suffer 99% of the casualties attributable to climate change. Poor people are more exposed and less able to cope with extremes, and poorer countries have fewer assets to adapt. A 2020 World Bank paper estimated climate change will push 32 million to 132 million more people into extreme poverty by 2030. Climate extremes could raise food prices by 3–84% by 2050. Adaptation that ignores how poverty differs from person to person will be ineffective and unfair. Pro-poor adaptation ties coping with climate change to reducing poverty.

nature-gov-173.title: Environmental racism
nature-gov-173.text: In 1982, protesting a PCB waste landfill in Warren County, North Carolina, Benjamin Chavis gave the problem a name: environmental racism. It means the heavier burden of pollution, hazards and ecological damage borne by marginalized communities and people of color. A US Government Accountability Office study after the protests was among the first to link the race and income of communities to hazardous waste sites. Causes include the hunt for cheap land, dismissive attitudes to harmful projects, and affected communities' lack of political power, mobility and money. It is built into policy at home and abroad, a form of structural racism that creates hierarchies of health. Some places, described in {{ref:nature-gov-224}}, absorb an outsized share of fossil fuel pollution. Some critics argue cost-benefit analysis feeds the problem, because it values resources by what people are willing to pay. The pattern crosses borders: between 1989 and 1994, an estimated 2,611 metric tons of hazardous waste went from OECD countries to poorer ones.

nature-gov-187.title: Climate change as a human rights issue
nature-gov-187.text: In 2005, Inuit activist Sheila Watt-Cloutier petitioned the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights over US contributions to global warming. The petition was rejected, but her testimony was later heard. Her case framed climate change as a human rights problem. Governments, UN bodies, advocates and scholars now use this framework to guide climate policy. Most statements stress threats to the rights to life, food, water, health, housing, development and self-determination. Human rights treaties rarely mention the environment, so protection is drawn from those rights. The UN Human Rights Council unanimously adopted Resolution 7/23, recognizing climate change as a threat to human rights. On 8 October 2021 it recognized a right to a safe, clean, healthy and sustainable environment. The stakes are large. The UN Development Programme estimates 600 million more people will face malnutrition because of climate change. Research suggests climate change may create some 50 to 200 million new displaced people by 2100.

nature-gov-222.title: The right to a healthy environment
nature-gov-222.text: For the first time, in 2021, the UN Human Rights Council recognized a human right in a resolution. The vote was 43 in favor, none against and 4 abstentions. The right was to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment, seen as necessary for the rights to life, health, food and water. The Council acted on 18 October 2021 and the General Assembly followed on 28 July 2022. That vote was 161 in favor, none against and eight abstentions, though such resolutions are not binding. 165 countries recognize the right in their constitutions, laws or ratified treaties. It protects nature through its effects on people, unlike traditional rules aimed at states or at nature itself. It obliges states to regulate polluters and enforce environmental law. It has also helped build precedent for climate lawsuits. The 1972 Stockholm conference's declaration had recognized it in its first principle, without binding force.

nature-gov-179.title: Access and benefit-sharing agreements
nature-gov-179.text: When a healer's knowledge leads a company to a valuable plant, who should be paid? An access and benefit-sharing agreement answers that, setting out how the benefits from using genetic resources are shared fairly. Such deals usually come from bioprospecting, the search for valuable compounds that Indigenous knowledge often guides. Before the Biodiversity Convention, plant genes were common heritage and freely exchanged. The convention gave each state sovereign rights over its own. The Nagoya Protocol, adopted in 2010 and in force from 2014, requires prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms. Benefits can be money, such as lump sums, milestone payments and royalties. They can also be shared research, joint patents, technology or training. Digital sequence data slips past this model, since no physical sample is needed. COP16 in Cali created a fund that gives half its resources to Indigenous peoples and local communities. Biodiversity-rich developing countries want stronger duties, while rich countries with big users of genetic resources prefer narrower ones.

openers.justice-rights-and-indigenous-knowledge: Environmental harm rarely lands evenly. Poor and marginalized communities often live beside the waste dumps, mines and polluting plants whose benefits flow elsewhere, and that grievance grew into a movement for environmental justice. Indigenous peoples sit at the center of this story: their lands are often where resources are pulled out for export, their knowledge of nature has been taken without permission, and they feel climate change more than most. Yet the same peoples, when their hold on land is secure, care for it in ways that benefit everyone. This chapter looks at who bears environmental costs, who gains, and what rights and laws people have used to fight back.
